title: Scalable integration of silicon carbide color centers into nanophotonic structures
authors: Raphael Wörnle, Jonas Schmid, Dennis Grüner, Jonah Heiler, Flavie Davidson-Marquis, Georgy V. Astakhov, Vadim Vorobyov, Florian Kaiser, Jonathan Körber, Jörg Wrachtrup
abstract: Color centers in silicon carbide are a promising platform for quantum technologies, offering long-coherence electron and nuclear spins for storing and manipulating quantum information, as well as single-photon emission for quantum communication. Low photon collection efficiency is commonly addressed by integrating color centers into nanophotonic devices. Here, we report a scalable method for the deterministic integration of color centers into silicon carbide nanopillars, using the same nanoscale mask for both implantation of oxygen-related color centers (PL5, PL6) and subsequent nanopillar fabrication via dry etching. This approach solves the issue of low color center creation yield in nanostructures, with figures of merit comparable to bulk samples. We demonstrate count rate enhancements of up to one order of magnitude for PL5 and four times for PL6, while preserving spin coherence times. Our method is directly applicable to other solid-state platforms, offering a scalable route to efficiently integrate color centers into nanostructures.
summary: This paper presents a scalable, deterministic fabrication technique to embed color centers in silicon carbide (SiC) nanopillars. By integrating ion implantation and dry etching using a single mask, the authors overcome low photon collection efficiency, achieving significant count rate enhancements while maintaining the quantum coherence properties of the emitters.
main_problem: The primary challenge addressed is overcoming the low photon collection efficiency when integrating color centers into nanophotonic structures for quantum applications.
main_result: The authors report a scalable, deterministic method to integrate color centers into SiC nanopillars, achieving count rate enhancements up to an order of magnitude while preserving spin coherence times.
method: The method combines deterministic ion implantation (using a patterned PMMA mask) with subsequent dry etching to define the nanopillar structure, enabling precise placement of quantum emitters.
model_or_system: The system utilizes color centers (PL5 and PL6) in silicon carbide (SiC) embedded within fabricated nanopillars. Characterization involves optical measurements (luminescence, ODMR) and quantum measurements ($g^{(2)}(0)$, $T_2$).
key_observables: Count rate enhancement factor, spin coherence time ($T_2$), second-order correlation function ($g^{(2)}(0)$), and defect creation yield.
important_parameters: Pillar dimensions (e.g., 200–900 nm diameter, $2.5\ \mu	ext{m}$ height), implantation ion species ($	ext{O}, 	ext{N}, 	ext{C}$), and annealing temperatures.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the PMMA mask defines both the implantation sites and the final nanopillar geometry, and that spin coherence times are preserved during the etching process.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the fabrication process flow, simulated count rate enhancements vs. pillar diameter, ODMR spectra, $g^{(2)}(0)$ measurements confirming single-emitter behavior, and $T_2$ measurements across different pillar types.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication process flow, starting with lithography and implantation, followed by etching to create nanopillars. Characterization proceeds by measuring optical enhancement, confirming single-photon emission statistics, and measuring spin coherence times, comparing results across bulk, membrane, and etched pillar geometries.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of coupling solid-state quantum emitters to photonic structures, which is crucial for building scalable quantum networks and quantum memories.
